title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks; 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed no verifier rejections: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was not invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0; bootstrap resamples=10,000, seed=1729). The preregistered generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false): the same single generated candidate was evaluated under both arms; this design decision is the proximate cause of the degenerate observed outcome and is documented with full execution provenance. We release the complete preregistration, execution traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest to enable deterministic reproduction and targeted follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Automation of network configuration from natural‑language intent using LLMs promises operational efficiency for NetOps but raises severe reliability and safety concerns: stochastic generation may yield syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe device commands. A pragmatic operational architecture is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): the generator proposes candidates, a deterministic verifier (oracle) checks safety/correctness, and a bounded repair loop attempts corrective generations guided by verifier diagnostics when needed. We preregistered a confirmatory paired study to quantify the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic network verifier into an LLM intent→configuration pipeline. The preregistered primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (the within‑task increase in detection/rejection proportion afforded by the guarded GVR arm versus generate‑only). All design elements, prompts, and execution artifacts were frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration JSON SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), i.e., a single generated candidate per task was evaluated in both baseline and guarded conditions; this decisive choice and its consequences are described explicitly below and in the Disclosure Statement (master prompt archive provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).
sections.related_work: Prior work frames GVR for safe code generation and compliance‑critical domains [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899]; formal network verification provides deterministic safety oracles for NetOps (NetKAT/weighted NetKAT and related decision procedures) [doi:10.1145/3808318]. Recent LLM‑for‑NetOps proposals highlight intent life‑cycle and RAG/agentic scaffolds for intent decomposition and verifier anchoring (examples: OpenAlex entries W4400072049, W4386722061). Our study differs: it is a preregistered, artifact‑backed, deterministic‑trace execution that measures the verifier’s marginal effect under explicitly recorded generation semantics. We do not benchmark model QA scores or claim production readiness; instead we publish exact execution provenance to enable deterministic replication and principled follow‑ups.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The full preregistration (machine‑readable) was frozen before execution (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design: paired within‑task. Task bank and sampling. SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1 (public synthetic intent→configuration suite produced and archived with the run) comprised N=270 tasks arranged as 3 vendor‑style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks per cell; 20% stratified validation subset (54 tasks) reserved to compute verifier‑emulator concordance metrics. Generator and verifier. Generator: gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses; declared_model_version gpt-5-mini; model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). Verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implemented on a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator, used as the deterministic oracle and emulator ground truth. Execution contract and decisive generation semantics. The registered execution_contract specified adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1, execution_mode scientific_confirmatory, model_names [gpt-5-mini], task_count 270, planned_episode_count 540, initial_generation_calls_per_task 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task 1, and independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics). This choice produced model_calls_used=270, i.e., one generation per pair that both arms evaluated; full execution manifest and hashes archived (execution/execution_manifest.json; raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a). Scoring, validation, and thresholds. Each candidate was validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with structured validation traces recorded in execution/scoring/*. Validation outputs include normalized_configuration, validator decision (valid/invalid), parsed_command_count, touched_field_count, and violation lists. The guarded arm policy was: if verifier rejects initial candidate invoke bounded repair loop (≤1 repair call) using the verifier diagnostics; repair prompt and repair traces are archived when invoked. Statistical analysis plan. Primary test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Missingness and retry policy. API call failures used preregistered deterministic retry policy (up to 2 retries per failed call); retries and any technical failures were logged (execution/execution_log.jsonl; artifact hashes provided). No post‑preregistration manual edits to manuscript technical content were permitted.

Observed operational outcome and causal account. The run produced a degenerate null: the verifier/repair pipeline was not invoked because the single generated candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics) was verifier‑acceptable for every task at the chosen generator settings. This is an artifact‑grounded fact documented in execution/* and analysis/* and is the proximate reason for the observed 100%/100% acceptance rates.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and limits of the observed null. The numerical p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are arithmetic consequences of zero discordant pairs (n10=n01=0) in the observed contingency table and therefore are degenerate in this execution. They do not imply that verifiers or GVR architectures lack utility in other evaluation regimes. The result demonstrates that two preregistered, artifact‑recorded factors jointly determined the outcome: (1) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced a single candidate per task evaluated under both arms (model_calls_used=270); (2) the chosen generator prompt/settings produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for these synthetic tasks. Both facts and their hashes are archived and verifiable (see execution/execution_manifest.json and model_configuration.json). Practical and operational implications. For operational NetOps risk management, the verifier’s real value arises when generators produce unverifiable or unsafe candidates (e.g., under higher sampling stochasticity, lower‑cost models, adversarial intents, or when tasks are more adversarial/complex). Our artifact bundle enables deterministic reproduction of this run and supports controlled variants that change only a single preregistered field (see reproducible follow‑up recipe below) to expose verifier utility. Reproducible follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored minimal change to test original estimand). The exact JSON fields to change in the preregistration/execution_contract are recorded in the frozen preregistration and execution_manifest; a minimal variant that validly tests the originally framed primary estimand is: (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true (currently false in the executed run) so that each arm receives an independent stochastic generation; (B) increase planned_model_calls or maximum_model_calls to 540 (one independent generation per condition per task) so that model_calls_used will permit independent sampling; (C) optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task to >1 to test bounded repair convergence; (D) vary generator stochasticity by setting model_configuration.temperature to non‑zero and provide a set of deterministic seeds in the task_manifest.task_payload (field names are present in the archived JSONs). All schema field names and paths are present in the archived preregistration and model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 a40e96e2...). These changes can be implemented reproducibly using the supplied harness without modifying verifier implementation. Threats to validity and how artifacts document them. Internal validity: deterministic shared_initial semantics directly limited variance and prevented between‑arm sampling; the decision was preregistered and is disclosed (preregistration SHA‑256 above). Construct validity: the synthetic task bank (SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1) captures many operational patterns (shutdown→change→restore, make‑before‑break), but remains synthetic; the emulator approximates device semantics but differs from heterogeneous production devices. External validity: single model (gpt-5-mini) and single verifier rule‑set were used; results do not generalize across models, rule sets, or adversarial inputs. Conclusion validity: the executed sampling plan (shared candidate) removes the stochastic variation that the original power calculation assumed; the preregistered MDE therefore does not apply to the observed numeric outcome. All these points are traceable to the archived preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We carried out a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline. Under the frozen shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings, the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for every one of N=270 tasks; verifier rejects and bounded repairs therefore did not occur, yielding a measured paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). This provenance‑backed null demonstrates that generation semantics and sampling variance are decisive experimental factors: when a generator consistently outputs acceptable candidates, an inserted deterministic verifier will not change accept/reject outcomes. We release the full preregistration, execution traces, validator/scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest so other researchers can (a) deterministically reproduce this run and (b) run the minimal variant specified above (independent_condition_generation=true, increased model_calls, varied seeds/temperature, larger repair budget) to measure verifier/repair utility under stochastic sampling and adversarial scenarios. Null results with full provenance are informative: they precisely delimit the evaluation regimes where an intervention changes behavior and where it does not. All experimental numbers and key artifacts are archived and referenced in the Disclosure Statement below.

Generation semantics (decisive): the registered and executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false) so that one generated candidate per paired task was evaluated by both arms; this is recorded in the preregistration and the execution manifest and is the proximate cause of the degenerate observed contingency (model_calls_used=270). Verifier and emulator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Dockerized Kathará/Mininet) served as the deterministic validator/emulator and as emulator ground truth; representative scoring artifacts are in execution/scoring/ (example SHA‑256s included in the manuscript). Tools and logging: the experiment harness logged all provider calls, raw responses, validator traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes; the full per‑artifact manifest is execution/execution_manifest.json and the raw results file execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 43381c4b07e1ffabb163657f56ae893fd65fc12d5307ea1ff3bb98f7cf43329a). Retry and failure policy: model/API call failures used the preregistered retry policy (up to 2 retries per failed call); in this run completed model_calls_used=270 and failed calls=0. Bounded repair budget: guarded arm allowed up to one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); no repairs were invoked because zero initial candidates were rejected. Autonomous peer review/revision: the AI performed internal automated peer review and produced the reviewer‑aware clarifications recorded in the revision instruction; the final manuscript text and references were produced autonomously after the autonomy lock. Limitations and threats: limitations enumerated in the manuscript (synthetic tasks, single model, generation semantics, limited repair budget, emulator↔production gap) are artifact‑grounded. All artifacts, code, and analysis logs necessary to deterministically reproduce and to run the minimal follow‑up variant (set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true; increase maximum_model_calls; increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task) are present in the execution bundle; see execution/* and analysis/*. No human manual technical edits occurred after autonomy lock; all logged hashes attest to the frozen pipeline.
limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogenous vendor devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality should be inferred.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered power/MDE calculation assumed independent sampling and is therefore inapplicable to the observed contingency.

Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
